name: Yedigöller National Park
desc: Seven small lakes strung down a forested valley, each one dammed by an old landslide and linked by short board-walk paths. Late October turns the beech and hornbeam into a wall of copper, and the reflection everyone photographs happens at Büyükgöl before nine in the morning. The rest of the year it is damp, quiet and full of birdsong.
season: Late Oct for colour, Jun–Sep for calm; the northern forest road is often snowbound Dec–Mar
tip: Come on a weekday — on autumn weekends the one-lane forest road from Bolu jams solid and you queue an hour just to park.
rev: Visitors agree the autumn colour matches the photographs, then complain about 40 km of rough forest road from Bolu, gridlock on October weekends, and litter around the main picnic lake.
entry: ≈₺120 (€2.50) per person plus a vehicle fee at the gate
onward: Istanbul (IST/SAW) or Ankara (ESB), then the motorway to Bolu and 40 km of forest road north — a car is the only realistic way in

name: Lake Abant
desc: A dark green lake at 1,300 m ringed by fir and beech, with a seven-kilometre path all the way round and horse-drawn phaetons clopping past the hotels. Weekends bring İstanbul families, gözleme stalls and woodsmoke; on a midweek morning in winter the surface freezes and the forest goes completely silent.
season: May–Jun for wildflowers, Oct for colour; Jul–Aug weekends are heaving
tip: Walk the far western shore — almost nobody gets past the first kilometre of stalls near the car park.
todo: Full circuit of the shore path
Phaeton ride to the far bank
rev: People love the walk and the air; recurring gripes are weekend crowds, overpriced hotel food, horses working in the heat, and a nature-park fee that keeps climbing.
entry: ≈₺100 (€2.20) per person, extra for a car
onward: Istanbul (IST/SAW) or Ankara (ESB) to Bolu, then 34 km on a good mountain road; weekend dolmuş from Bolu otogar

name: Gölcük Lake
desc: A small dark lake in the fir forest 15 km south of Bolu, circled by a wooden walkway you can cover in half an hour. Half-drowned trunks stand out of the shallows and the mist usually sits on the water until the sun clears the ridge. It is the easiest piece of proper forest near the İstanbul–Ankara motorway.
season: May–Oct; snow closes the last stretch of road most winters
tip: Weekday mornings only — at weekends the walkway is a wedding-photo conveyor belt.
todo: Aladağ pine track above the park
rev: Called a perfect two-hour stop by most who go, with the usual complaints about weekend picnic crowds, loud music from the car park and a fee for what is essentially a short stroll.
onward: Istanbul (IST/SAW) or Ankara (ESB) to Bolu, then 13 km up the Aladağ road; taxi from Bolu is cheap

name: Mudurnu
desc: An Ottoman market town folded into a valley, where the medieval craftsmen's guild still opens the week with a prayer over the shopkeepers' takings. Timber-framed houses lean over stone lanes, Yıldırım Bayezid's 1382 hamam still takes bathers, and the Armutçular konak shows the tall dark rooms behind those façades.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; winter is grey and half the konaks shut
tip: Be in the Yıldırım Bayezid mosque courtyard early on a Friday for the ahi guild ceremony — it is not staged for visitors.
rev: Visitors call it the least touristed Ottoman town within three hours of İstanbul, while noting that restoration is patchy, several konaks are locked with no keyholder in sight, and there is very little to eat after dark.
onward: Istanbul (IST/SAW), motorway to Bolu, then 52 km south over the pass; hourly dolmuş from Bolu otogar

name: Göynük
desc: White houses with black timber frames stacked up a hillside above a stream, restored hard over the last decade and used as a set for period television. Akşemseddin, the teacher of Mehmed the Conqueror, is buried at the top of the thousand-step stone stair, and the small covered market still sells the local pear and pastırma.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov; midsummer is hot in the valley
tip: Climb to the Zafer clock tower at dusk, when the whole white-and-black grid below switches its lights on.
todo: Thousand steps to the clock tower
rev: Most reports praise the restored streets and the quiet, but a fair number find the make-over too uniform, the museums shut outside summer, and weekend day-trip buses filling the one main lane.
onward: Istanbul (IST/SAW), motorway to Düzce or Bolu, then about an hour south; dolmuş from Bolu and Adapazarı

name: Kartalkaya
desc: Bolu's ski mountain, 1,850 to 2,200 m of fir forest and open bowl on the Köroğlu range, with two hotel clusters and lifts that run straight from the door. Snow is reliable from late December, the runs are short but tree-lined, and it is the closest proper skiing to İstanbul at roughly three and a half hours.
season: Late Dec–mid Mar for snow; in summer the ridge is empty grazing land with paragliding launches
tip: Buy a day pass at the smaller Kartal side rather than the big resort — same lifts, shorter queues, cheaper lunch.
todo: Ridge run through the fir belt
rev: Skiers rate the tree runs and the short transfer from İstanbul, then complain about half-term lift queues, dated hotel packages with compulsory full board, and a road up that needs chains after every fresh fall.
entry: Day lift pass ≈₺1,500 (€32); hotels sell all-in packages
onward: Istanbul (IST/SAW) or Ankara (ESB) to Bolu, then 38 km of switchbacks; hotel shuttles meet buses at Bolu otogar

name: Sülüklü Lake
desc: A leech-named tarn at 1,450 m in the fir forest above Mudurnu, reached by a dozen kilometres of forest track that turns to mud after rain. Dead trunks stand in black water, fog rolls in most afternoons, and it is one of the few places within four hours of İstanbul where you can camp and hear nothing at all.
season: Jun–Sep; the track is impassable with snow or heavy rain
tip: The final eight kilometres need clearance and dry weather — after rain the villagers tell you to walk it, and they are right.
todo: Camp a night by the water
Sunrise fog over the dead trunks
rev: Campers describe it as genuinely wild and eerily quiet; the complaints are the state of the access track, rubbish left by weekend groups, mosquitoes in July and no facilities of any kind.
onward: Istanbul (IST/SAW), motorway to Bolu, then Mudurnu and 20 km of forest track — high clearance strongly advised

name: Samandere Waterfall
desc: A twenty-metre fall dropping into a mossy basalt slot in dense beech forest, reached by a few hundred wooden steps down from the road. Spray keeps the rock slick and the air cold even in August. Protected as a natural monument since 1988, with trout restaurants at the top that are half the reason people stop.
season: Apr–Jun at full flow; Sep–Oct for the colour, thin water by late summer
tip: Skip the crowded lower platform and follow the path 200 m upstream to the second cascade, where almost nobody goes.
todo: Steps down to the plunge pool
rev: Reports call it a genuinely pretty half-hour, spoiled on summer weekends by picnic crowds on the narrow stairs, slippery unrailed rock and a car park that fills before ten.
onward: Istanbul (IST/SAW), motorway to Düzce, then 25 km south through the villages; no useful public transport

name: Güzeldere Waterfall
desc: A hundred-metre ribbon down a black rock face in the forest above Gölyaka, seen either from a platform level with the lip or from the bottom of some seven hundred wooden steps. In spring it thunders and soaks the viewing deck; by late August it is a thin veil. The drive up through hazel groves is half the outing.
season: Apr–Jun for volume; Oct for colour; the road ices over in winter
tip: Take the upper platform first for the whole drop, then decide whether your knees want the steps down and back up.
todo: Upper platform for the full drop
rev: Visitors are impressed by the height and unimpressed by the climb back, the state of some of the steps, and how little water is left after July.
onward: Istanbul (IST/SAW), motorway to Düzce, then 30 km via Gölyaka on a narrow paved road

name: Akçakoca
desc: Düzce's seaside town: hazelnut hills running down to a long grey-sand shore, a Genoese castle ruin on the Ceneviz headland and a row of fish restaurants along the front. The water is cold and honest, the surf can turn dangerous within an hour, and the whole place empties after mid-September.
season: Jul–Aug for swimming; the sea here rarely passes 22 °C
tip: Drive 6 km west to Karaburun for the lighthouse and a beach without loudspeakers.
todo: Hamsi and cornbread on the front
rev: Weekenders like the cheap fish and the short drive from İstanbul; the constant complaints are rip currents and drownings on unpatrolled stretches, concrete blocks along the shore and August crowds.
onward: Istanbul (IST/SAW), motorway to Düzce, then 38 km north over the hazelnut ridge; frequent dolmuş from Düzce otogar

name: Topuk Yayla
desc: A high meadow above the Bolu Dağı tunnels with a small lake, a boardwalk, horses grazing and a resort hotel that put the place on the map. The forest tracks beyond the gate are free and usually empty, and on most mornings the cloud sits in the valley below while the plateau is in sun.
season: May–Oct for the meadow; Dec–Feb for snow, when the access road needs care
tip: The lakeside path and picnic meadows are public — park below the hotel gate rather than paying for anything.
rev: Guests rate the setting and the cool air highly, while day visitors report feeling pushed toward hotel prices, a small lake that underwhelms in dry summers, and mud everywhere after rain.
entry: Free for the public meadow and lake path
onward: Istanbul (IST/SAW), motorway to the Bolu Dağı exit, then 12 km up a paved forest road

name: Gökgöl Cave
desc: Three kilometres of active river cave right beside the Zonguldak–Ankara road, of which about a kilometre is lit and walkable on steel catwalks. Curtain formations, a permanent stream running under your feet and a constant 12 °C. It is one of the easiest big caves in the country to visit and takes roughly forty minutes.
season: All year; spring meltwater can close the lower gallery
tip: Bring a fleece and shoes with grip — the air stays around 12 °C and the walkway drips the entire way.
todo: Lit gallery to the far chamber
rev: Rated a good-value stop with well-built walkways, though visitors mention harsh coloured lighting, a short circuit for the ticket, and closures after heavy rain that are not posted anywhere.
onward: Zonguldak Çaycuma (ONQ) airport 40 min, or Istanbul then the coast road; the cave sits 4 km east of Zonguldak on the D-750

name: Cehennemağzı Caves
desc: Three caves above Karadeniz Ereğli that antiquity called a mouth of Hades — the place where Heracles was said to have dragged up Cerberus. The middle one was used as a chapel by early Christians and keeps a rock-cut altar and a spring; Byzantine scratchings survive on the walls. Small, strange, ten minutes from the town centre.
season: All year; the steps are slick after rain
tip: Ask at the ticket hut to have the lights switched on in the third cave — it is usually left dark and people miss it entirely.
todo: Rock-cut altar in the chapel cave
Ereğli museum in the old Greek school
rev: Visitors find the mythology and the chapel worth the short stop but describe the site as neglected, poorly lit and hemmed in by housing, with a strong smell of damp in the lower cave.
onward: Zonguldak (ONQ) airport 50 min, or Istanbul and 3 h by coach to Ereğli; the caves are a short taxi ride from the otogar

name: Tios (Filyos)
desc: A Greek colony on a bluff where the Filyos river meets the sea, dug slowly since 2006: a Roman theatre, a bath complex, stretches of city wall and a gate that looks straight out at the surf. The site is unfenced and half-overgrown, sharing its headland with a fishing hamlet and an enormous new port under construction downstream.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the headland is exposed and wet in winter
tip: Go for the last hour of daylight — the theatre faces west over the river mouth, and there is no lighting or staff after dark.
todo: Roman theatre above the river mouth
rev: Those who make the detour like having a Roman theatre entirely to themselves, but report no signage, waist-high weeds in summer, active trenches fenced off, and the port works dominating the view.
onward: Zonguldak Çaycuma (ONQ) airport 25 min, then the coast road to Filyos; buses from Zonguldak run to Çaycuma only

name: Amasra
desc: A Byzantine-walled town on a rock tied to the mainland by a Roman bridge, with two harbours — one for boats, one for swimming — and a Genoese citadel that people still live inside. The small museum holds Roman marble dug out of back gardens. Everything smells of fried hamsi and the woodcarvers' workshops.
season: Jun–Sep for the water; on Jul–Aug weekends the causeway becomes a car park
tip: Cross the Kemere bridge to Boztepe and walk out to the Kuşkayası Roman road monument early, before the Safranbolu buses arrive at eleven.
todo: Fish and salad at Küçük Liman
rev: Almost everyone rates the setting and the fish, then warns about August gridlock on the single access road, restaurant bills that arrive higher than the menu suggests, and a crowded, stony town beach.
entry: Town free; museum ≈₺60 (€1.30) · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Zonguldak (ONQ) airport then 90 min, or Ankara (ESB) and 4.5 h via Karabük; daily buses from Safranbolu

name: Kurucaşile
desc: A one-street coastal town that has built wooden boats for centuries — yards along the shore still lay keels by eye, and the smell of larch and pitch carries up the road. Beyond it the coast east toward Cide is among the emptiest and most twisting stretches of the whole Black Sea shore.
season: Jun–Sep; the coast road is landslide-prone after winter storms
tip: Walk into a boatyard and ask — the builders are used to visitors and will happily show you a hull in frame.
rev: Travellers describe an unspoiled working town with real character, while noting there is almost nothing to do after dark, few beds, and a coast road that takes far longer than the map suggests.
onward: Zonguldak (ONQ) airport then 2 h via Amasra, or Kastamonu (KFS) and 3 h through Cide; minibuses from Bartın

name: İnkumu
desc: Bartın's own beach: two kilometres of pale sand backed by pines, shallow enough for small children and full of Bartın families from July. Four kilometres west, the Güzelcehisar basalt columns rise straight out of the shore — a wall of hexagonal lava pillars with a viewing platform above and almost nobody on it.
season: Jul–Aug for swimming; May–Jun and Sep for the walk and the columns
tip: Drive on to Güzelcehisar for the basalt cliffs — free, signposted badly and usually empty even in August.
todo: Swim off the sandy west end
rev: Families rate the safe shallow water and cheap pensions; complaints run to summer-weekend crowding, thin sand in places, and litter after busy days.
onward: Zonguldak (ONQ) airport 1 h, or Ankara (ESB) 4.5 h; frequent dolmuş from Bartın centre, 12 km

name: Küre Mountains National Park
desc: A karst massif of beech and fir between Bartın and Kastamonu, protected as one of Europe's PAN Parks: sinkholes, underground rivers and canyons cutting four hundred metres deep. Ulukaya waterfall, the Ilgarini cave and the Valla rim all sit inside it, and bears and wolves are genuinely present rather than notional.
season: May–Oct; forest tracks are impassable with snow Dec–Mar
tip: Base yourself in Azdavay or Pınarbaşı rather than Bartın — the trailheads, guides and village guesthouses are all on the Kastamonu side.
rev: Walkers praise genuinely wild forest and near-total solitude, while flagging unmarked trails, no rescue infrastructure, tick-heavy undergrowth in summer and villages where nobody speaks English.
onward: Kastamonu (KFS) airport, then the Azdavay or Pınarbaşı road; from the Bartın side the Ulus forest road is slow and unpaved in places

name: Safranbolu
desc: An Ottoman caravan town of around two thousand timber-and-plaster houses, preserved whole because the railway and the road both went elsewhere. The Cinci Han still stands over a market of coppersmiths and saddlers, the Kaymakamlar house shows how a merchant family actually lived, and the whole bowl is best read from Hıdırlık hill.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; snow suits the town but closes several konaks
tip: Stay the night — the day-trip coaches leave by five and the old town becomes a completely different, empty place.
rev: Widely rated the best-preserved Ottoman town in Türkiye, with steady complaints about souvenir shops selling the same Turkish delight, coach groups filling the square by mid-morning, and steep cobbles that punish bad shoes.
entry: Town free; each konak-museum ≈₺60 (€1.30) · Museum Pass Türkiye valid at the state museums
onward: Ankara (ESB) then 3 h by road or bus to Karabük; Kastamonu (KFS) airport is a 2 h drive

name: Yörük Köyü
desc: A stone-and-timber village twelve kilometres east of Safranbolu, settled by Yörük nomads and left almost untouched: a communal laundry with its stone basins still in place, a square of blackened konaks, and the Sipahioğlu house opened by the family that owns it. Perhaps thirty people live here through the winter.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; very quiet and often shut in midwinter
tip: Knock at the Sipahioğlu Konağı rather than waiting for a guide — the owners show you the hidden women's gallery themselves.
todo: Village bread oven and tea house
rev: Visitors call it Safranbolu without the crowds and with more honest decay; the flip side is that half the houses are locked, restoration money is visibly thin, and there is nowhere to eat beyond one tea garden.
onward: Ankara (ESB) then Karabük; from Safranbolu it is 12 km by taxi or the Konarı dolmuş
